newsitem.title: USA: Tax week on Capitol Hill brings flurry of activity.
newsitem.headline: Tax week on Capitol Hill brings flurry of activity.

text.p: Tax week on Capitol Hill promises to generate a flurry of activity as lawmakers try to assure the public they feel their pain at tax time.
The April 15 tax filing deadline has been set as a marker for some bill introductions and votes on tax-related issues.
At least two pieces of tax-type legislation are expected to go before the House of Representatives for a vote Tuesday.
One would be an amendment to the U.S. Constitution that would require a two-thirds vote of Congress to pass a tax increase, except in the case of war or national emergency.
The amendment itself would require a two-thirds vote in the House and Senate, but even supporters said that it was unlikely to pass this time around.
"I don't expect it to pass this April 15, but there will be a vote every April 15," Grover Norquist, president of Americans for Tax Reform, said.
Another bill likely to go before the full House would create criminal penalties for Internal Revenue Service (IRS) employees who snoop through taxpayer files.
The anti-browsing legislation would institute a punishment for unauthorized peeking at taxpayer files of a fine up to $100,000 and/or imprisonment of not more than one year.
It would also require the IRS to notify the victim of unauthorized browsing and allow victims to seek civil penalties. Treasury officials have said they support the legislation.
Sen. Paul Coverdell has introduced a similar bill in the Senate which is also expected to be brought up in that chamber next week, a spokesman for the Georgia Republican said.

Sen. John Ashcroft and Rep. George Nethercutt, a Washington Republican, planned to introduce a bill in their respective chambers to end what they called "double-taxation" by allowing the Social Security payroll tax to be deducted from gross income.

Ashcroft, a Missouri Republican, said the legislation would result in a $228 billion reduction in federal government revenues over five years, but if it were phased in the cost could be reduced to about $116 billion.
"That (phase-in) would put us more directly in the ballpark of the expected capacity for tax relief this year," he said.
Republicans are seeking tax cuts in this year's budget negotiations that are bigger than President Clinton has proposed.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich came out strongly for a tax cut saying he favored abolishing the capital gains and inheritance taxes altogether.
Gingrich had come under fire from conservatives within his party last month when he suggested holding off discussing tax cuts until after a balanced budget was worked out.
The Georgia Republican more recently said he will put a tax cutting package to a vote by October regardless of whether an agreement is reached with the White House.

On Tuesday, Republican leaders will participate in a two-hour forum at the Capitol on tax relief. Attendees will include Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi, and House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas.
